metadata.title: Claude, Chronology.
metadata.purpose: Answer what a case chronology actually is, once you have a stack of documents that each mention dates on their own: a plain sorted list, or something else. Lands the carry-out that a chronology is each event named once, no matter how many documents mention it, weighed by what the case is trying to prove.

beats.narration_text: The instinct with a chronology is to sort every date the file mentions. Here's what's actually happening: that plain sort counts the same event twice, and never asks which dates weigh on the case.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Just sort every date?', hesitates on 'sort', corrects to 'weigh', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('sort' -> 'weigh') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A matter's facts sit inside a stack of documents — emails, invoices, deposition transcripts — each one mentioning dates on its own. The obvious move is to pull every date out and lay them in order. Here's what's actually happening when you do: two documents can describe the exact same event, on the exact same day, in different words, and a plain list scores that as two things. It's optimized for completeness. What it sacrifices is any sense of what actually happened.

shot.new_visual_element: A sorted date list fed by three source chips; two cards land on the same day, worded differently, sitting side by side -- visibly duplicated

production_viz.label: A plain list counts twice
production_viz.mechanic: Three source chips (EMAIL / INVOICE / DEPOSITION) each drop a dated card into a single sorted list running top to bottom. Two of the cards land at the same vertical position (same day), worded differently, and sit side by side in the list -- visibly duplicated. A caption fades in beneath: 'one event, counted twice.'

beats.narration_text: Chronology building rewires the sort. It pulls every dated event out of the declared sources, then collapses the duplicates — however many documents name the same event, it becomes one entry. Watch one event go through the machinery. A late payment. An email flags it. An invoice restates it. A deposition describes it again, in different words, same day. Three mentions collapse into one thing that actually happened.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three source cards (EMAIL / INVOICE / DEPOSITION), same date stamped on each, collapsing into one card: LATE PAYMENT -- ONE ENTRY

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three sources, one entry
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards labelled 'EMAIL', 'INVOICE', 'DEPOSITION', each stamped the same date, slide toward center and collapse into a single card reading 'LATE PAYMENT -- ONE ENTRY'. THIS EXACT COLLAPSE RETURNS, TAGGED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: One entry, not three — that part doesn't change. What changes is the tag on it. For a matter built on breach of contract, that late payment is central, tagged high. For a different matter, built on a different theory, the same payment barely registers, tagged low. Here's the design choice: the events are shared, the weights are not. A low tag doesn't mean the event is wrong or missing — it means this matter's theory doesn't turn on it. And one entry instead of three doesn't mean only one document mentioned it — it means every mention pointed at the exact same day.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the collapsed card splits into two tagged copies: BREACH-OF-CONTRACT MATTER: HIGH (terracotta) and A DIFFERENT MATTER: LOW (dimmed)

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- same event, different tag
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 THREE-CARD COLLAPSE RETURNS, identical placement, then splits into two tagged copies: left card 'BREACH-OF-CONTRACT MATTER' with 'LATE PAYMENT: HIGH' highlighted terracotta; right card 'A DIFFERENT MATTER' with 'LATE PAYMENT: LOW', dimmed. A caption underneath: 'same event, different tag.'

beats.narration_text: A chronology isn't every date in order — it's each event named once, no matter how many documents mention it, and weighed by what this case is trying to prove.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I have a stack of documents from a legal matter — emails, invoices, deposition transcripts, whatever's been produced. Pull every dated event out of them, collapse anything that's really the same event on the same day into one entry no matter how many documents mention it, then flag which entries actually matter to how this case is being argued and which barely register, given the matter's theory. Go deeper: for one entry the model flagged as barely mattering, ask what would have to change about the case's theory for that same event to suddenly be central. Liam, in for Bear.
